Summary:

The revised manuscript addresses most concerns of the reviewers and is thus of great interest. There remain some concerns to be addressed as detailed below.

Essential revisions:

1) The authors need to clarify the results in Figure 2B (right panel) and Figure 2F. In Figure 2B, the exogenously added CTLs exhibit swarming (increased FMI) towards the cognate tumour even in the absence of pre-embedded antigen-specific CTLs. However, in Figure 2F, exogenously added CTLs do not exhibit swarming unless there are pre-embedded antigen-specific CTLs. What is the cause of this discrepancy?

2) Subsection “CTL recruitment is driven by secretion of CCL3 and CCL4” – Clarification is required. The authors state "only CCL3 and CCL4 inhibition disrupted CTL transmigration towards cognate supernatants." However, in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, CCL4 blocking Abs alone have no effect on transmigration, despite that fact that both CCL3 and CCL4 blocking antibodies are required to block directional migration in Figure 4G. Can the authors provide an explanation for this discrepancy in the text?

3) Figure 5F – OT1 WT and OT1 CCR5-/- both exhibit a large increase in recruitment to the tumour when gBT1 cells are pre-transferred. This observation suggests that CCL3 and CCL4 actually play a very minor role in T cell "swarming" in this in vivo system. The authors should alter the wording of the abstract since it currently states that "CTLs engaging cognate targets accelerate the recruitment of distant T cells through long-range homotypic signalling via the diffusion of secreted chemokines CCL3 and CCL4". This statement suggests that CCL3/CCL4 play a major role in T cell swarming, but this claim isn't fully supported by the in vivo data.

This high transfer number may diminish the role of CCR5/CCL3/CCL4 mediated recruitment of CTLs into the tumour in vivo. At the very least, the authors should comment on this issue in the text.

Overexpression of CCL3/4 in the tumors seems to have no effect (at least statistically) on the recruitment of OT1 CTLs or endogenous CTLS into the tumor in vivo. claims.claim: The individuals of a CTL population exist in three distinct states: a 'searcher' state, a 'responder' state, and an 'engager/recruiter' state.
claims.source: We thus propose that the individuals of a CTL population exist in three distinct states: a 'searcher' state whilst scanning for cognate antigen unaffected by the homotypic signal; a 'responder' state when they sense the homotypic signal and move rapidly towards the effector locus; and an 'engager/recruiter' state upon target cell recognition when they concurrently deliver their effector function and secrete CCL3 and CCL4 (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The first CTLs to recognise a cognate target directly transition from search into engagement and recruitment.
claims.source: The first CTLs to recognise a cognate target directly transition from search into engagement and recruitment, whereas subsequent cells arrive in a responder state.
claims.evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claims.claim: CTLs can remain in an exclusive recruiter state for nearly 24 hr following target elimination in the absence of active engagement.
claims.source: It is interesting to note that CTLs can also remain in an exclusive recruiter state for nearly 24 hr following target elimination in the absence of active engagement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I).
claims.evidence: This observation is stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I.

claims.claim: The multistate recruitment model explains prior observations of non-specific T cells only deeply infiltrating tumour tissues in the presence of tumour-reactive CTLs.
claims.source: This multistate recruitment model explains prior observations of non-specific T cells only deeply infiltrating tumour tissues in the presence of tumour-reactive CTLs (Boissonnas et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Boissonnas et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Although antigen recognition is specific, the chemoattractive signal that is raised to amplify recruitment is generic and thus able to recruit a repertoire of CTLs regardless of their TCR specificity.
claims.source: Although antigen recognition is specific, the chemoattractive signal that is raised to amplify recruitment is generic and thus able to recruit a repertoire of CTLs regardless of their TCR specificity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: There have been prior observations of bystander recruitment of effector T cells to sites of inflammation or tumours initiated by unrelated antigen.
claims.source: Indeed, there have been prior observations of bystander recruitment of effector T cells to sites of inflammation or tumours initiated by unrelated antigen (Boissonnas et al., 2004; Topham et al., 2001; Ariotti et al., 2015; Hickman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Studies that compared tumours infiltrated by leukocytes ('hot') to those that excluded immune cell infiltration ('cold') identified more abundant CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in hot tumours.
claims.source: Interestingly, studies that compared tumours infiltrated by leukocytes ('hot') to those that excluded immune cell infiltration ('cold') identified more abundant CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in hot tumours (Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Spranger et al., 2015), including via single-cell transcriptomics that ascribed their expression to CD8+ T cells (Jerby-Arnon et al., 2018; Roider et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: CTLs exhibit chemotaxis towards CCR5 ligands within dense tumour tissue by intravital imaging.
claims.source: We demonstrated that CTLs exhibit chemotaxis towards CCR5 ligands within dense tumour tissue by intravital imaging, and revealed that the presence of antigen-specific CTLs within a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CTLs into the tumour in a manner partially dependent on CCR5.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the in vivo findings.

claims.claim: The presence of antigen-specific CTLs within a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CTLs into the tumour in a manner partially dependent on CCR5.
claims.source: We demonstrated that CTLs exhibit chemotaxis towards CCR5 ligands within dense tumour tissue by intravital imaging, and revealed that the presence of antigen-specific CTLs within a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CTLs into the tumour in a manner partially dependent on CCR5.

claims.claim: The activation of intratumoural CTLs promotes the recruitment of not only CTLs, but also natural killer cells and myeloid cells.
claims.source: The activation of intratumoural CTLs were found by others to promote the recruitment of not only CTLs, but also natural killer cells and myeloid cells (Rosato et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosato et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Alternate chemokine signalling circuits centred on CXCR3 and BLT1 have been implicated in CTL tumour trafficking and infiltration.
claims.source: Alternate chemokine signalling circuits centred on CXCR3 and BLT1 have been implicated in CTL tumour trafficking and infiltration (Chheda et al., 2016; Chow et al., 2019; Mikucki et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: IFNγ can induce CXCL9 and CXCL10 secretion in various intermediary cells, including tumour-infiltrating myeloid cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, IFNγ, produced by activated CTLs and abundant in inflamed tumours, can induce CXCL9 and CXCL10 secretion in various intermediary cells, including tumour-infiltrating myeloid cells (Dobrzanski et al., 2001; Gordon-Alonso et al., 2017; Hickman et al., 2015), which may enhance the role of CXCR3 in homing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: CCR5-expressing CTLs have been associated with severe autoimmune diseases.
claims.source: CCR5-expressing CTLs have been associated with severe autoimmune diseases (Mackay, 2014), and CCR5 ligands are abundant in the upper respiratory tract during acute hyperinflammation associated with viral infection (Chua et al., 2020); silencing homotypic recruitment may well prove beneficial in such contexts.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mackay, 2014 and Chua et al., 2020.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chua et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The homotypic recruitment mechanism could be exploited to enhance control over positioning and tissue infiltration of T cells in adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies.
claims.source: Ultimately, the homotypic recruitment mechanism could be exploited to enhance control over positioning and tissue infiltration of T cells in adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies, not least given our findings that engineered CAR T cells, following antigen recognition via the CAR, are able to induce homotypic recruitment of distal T cell populations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

results.result: Primary murine CTLs exhibit swarming behavior towards cognate tumouroids, accumulating at the edge over time. This behavior is reminiscent of neutrophil swarming and requires cognate antigen recognition. Enhanced infiltration occurs when additional CTLs are pre-embedded in the tumouroid, and computational modeling with a desensitization threshold recapitulates experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C20 collectively demonstrate CTL swarming through experimental observations (Figures 1B, Videos 1-3) and computational modeling (Figure 1F-G, Video 4). The behavior is antigen-dependent (C17), enhanced by pre-embedded CTLs (C18-C19), and requires desensitization mechanisms in simulations (C20). Multiple independent lines of evidence converge to support this novel finding.

results.result: CTLs migrate rapidly and directionally towards cognate tumour masses through homotypic signaling mediated by diffusible factors. Cell-free supernatant from CTL-cognate target co-incubation attracts other CTLs, and this recruitment is preserved when tumour cells are replaced with cognate antigen-coated beads, demonstrating that CTLs themselves produce the chemoattractant factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 are well-supported by multiple experimental approaches including direct migration assays (Figure 2B), transwell assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C), and bead replacement experiments (Figure 2C-D). The high sensitivity to diluted supernatants (C24) and preservation with beads (C25) provide strong evidence for CTL-derived homotypic signaling (C26).

results.result: The homotypic recruitment signal is antigen-specific in its production but generic in its effect, recruiting CTLs regardless of their TCR specificity. Tumouroids containing monospecific CTLs engaging cognate targets recruit T cells of the same, different, and polyclonal specificities equally, while no recruitment occurs towards CTLs engaging non-cognate targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by experiments showing recruitment of OT1, gBT1, and polyclonal T cells towards tumouroids containing different CTL specificities (Figures 2E-G). The requirement for cognate antigen recognition for signal production (C28) combined with TCR-independent recruitment (C27, C29) is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Long-range chemotactic gradients emanate from CTLs engaging cognate tumouroids, inducing directional migration in CTLs up to 1.6 mm away. CTLs close to the tumouroid lose directionality over time, possibly due to excess ligand concentration, while distant CTLs begin directional migration at later timepoints, revealing a moving wave of chemoattraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 are supported by detailed spatiotemporal analysis (Figure 3A-E, Video 6) showing initial uniform distribution (C30), progressive bias towards cognate tumouroids (C31), directional movement of distant cells (C32), and temporal dynamics of chemotaxis (C33, C35). The desensitization hypothesis (C34) is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2018, and the overall conclusion of gradient formation (C36) is well-justified.

results.result: GPCR ligands, specifically chemokines rather than lipid signals, mediate the chemoattractive signal in CTL swarming. Pertussis toxin (PTX) inhibits both enhanced speed and directional migration of CTLs towards cognate tumouroids, indicating GPCR involvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 are supported by PTX inhibition experiments (Figure 4A) and comparison with neutrophil swarming mechanisms (C40, citation to Lämmermann et al., 2013). The conclusion that chemokines underpin homotypic signaling (C41) is well-supported by the PTX data and consistent with prior work on CTL clustering (C39, Cockburn et al., 2013).

results.result: CCL3 and CCL4 are the key chemokines mediating CTL homotypic recruitment. These chemokines are differentially expressed at both mRNA (RNA-seq) and protein (mass spectrometry) levels in CTLs engaging cognate targets. Directional migration in 3D matrices is abolished only when both CCL3 and CCL4 are blocked simultaneously, indicating functional redundancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are strongly supported by multiple complementary approaches: RNA-seq (Figure 4B), mass spectrometry (Figure 4C), qRT-PCR validation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B), and functional neutralization experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-G). The requirement for dual blockade (C46) demonstrates redundancy, and the conclusion that CCL3/CCL4 constitute the homotypic signal (C47) is well-justified.

results.result: Secreted CCL3 forms a spatial gradient from sites of antigen-specific engagement, and CTLs sustain chemokine secretion even after target disengagement. Tumour cells engineered to constitutively secrete CCL3/CCL4 induce CTL swarming and infiltration comparable to tumouroids with actively engaged CTLs, confirming sufficiency of these chemokines.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by in situ gradient visualization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C), time-course secretion analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-I), and engineered tumour cell experiments (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3). The sustained secretion after disengagement (C49) and sufficiency of CCL3/CCL4 (C50-C51) provide strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: CCR5 mediates the chemokine signal underpinning homotypic CTL recruitment. Pharmacological inhibition with Maraviroc or Cenicriviroc, and genetic deletion of Ccr5, abrogate CTL recruitment, swarming, and infiltration. Ccr5-/- CTLs retain normal cytotoxicity and chemokine secretion, indicating a specific defect in chemokine sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 are strongly supported by pharmacological inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C), Ccr5-/- experiments (Figures 5A-D), and functional validation showing preserved cytotoxicity and secretion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-I). The convergence of pharmacological and genetic approaches provides robust evidence for CCR5's role (C61).

results.result: In vivo, CCR5 mediates CTL homing to CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours and recruitment through dense tumour tissue. The presence of tumour-reactive CTLs promotes recruitment of distant CCR5+ CTLs into tumours. However, Ccr5-/- CTLs clear tumours with comparable efficacy to WT CTLs, suggesting CCR5-independent mechanisms also contribute to tumour clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C69 are supported by in vivo adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-F), intravital imaging with CCL3-containing hydrogel (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Video 7), and tumour clearance assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G). The comparable tumour clearance by Ccr5-/- CTLs (C67) appropriately qualifies the role of CCR5 as important but not exclusive (C68-C69).

results.result: Human effector T cells and CAR T cells employ homotypic chemokine signaling to drive rapid convergence. Activated human T cells upregulate CCL3/CCL4 and produce chemoattractive supernatant. EphA2-specific CAR T cells swarm towards tumouroids containing glioblastoma cells but not EphA2-negative fibroblasts, and this recruitment is abolished by Cenicriviroc.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 are supported by experiments with primary human T cells (Figure 6A-F, Video 8) and CAR T cells (Figure 6G-I, Video 9). The antigen-specificity (C76-C77), CCR5-dependence (C74), and functional cytotoxicity (C75) are well-demonstrated. This extends the murine findings to clinically relevant human systems.

results.result: CTLs engaging targets employ homotypic signaling via CCL3/CCL4 secretion to accelerate recruitment of distant T cells in a positive feedback loop leading to swarming. CTLs closest to the chemotactic source become desensitized over time, losing directional bias, possibly due to excess ligand or CCR5 internalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 synthesize the major findings into a coherent mechanistic model. The positive feedback mechanism (C81) is supported by the cumulative experimental evidence. The desensitization observation (C82) is supported by data (Figure 3E) and citations to Lim et al., 2018 and Escola et al., 2010, though the specific mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: A three-state model is proposed for CTL populations: 'searcher' (scanning for antigen), 'responder' (sensing homotypic signal and migrating towards effector locus), and 'engager/recruiter' (recognizing targets while secreting CCL3/CCL4). Only CTLs directly engaging cognate antigen secrete the recruitment signal, and CTLs can remain in a recruiter state for ~24 hours after target elimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 present a conceptual model (Figure 7) synthesizing the experimental findings. The requirement for direct engagement (C89) is supported by data showing unconjugated CTLs don't upregulate chemokines (C90, Supplementary files 1-2). The sustained recruiter state (C93) is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-I. While the three-state model (C91-C92) is inferential, it is well-grounded in the data.

results.result: CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours recruit more endogenous NK cells than control tumours in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by in vivo experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B) showing consistent recruitment of NK cells to CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours. This demonstrates that the homotypic signaling mechanism can recruit other immune cell types beyond CTLs.

results.result: CTLs are key effectors of adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies, but their efficacy remains limited with solid tumours, which they infiltrate in insufficient numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 provide background context supported by appropriate citations (Guedan et al., 2019; van der Woude et al., 2017; Galon et al., 2006). These establish the clinical motivation for the study but are not novel findings of this work.

results.result: Prior work has shown that CTLs arrive at target sites via random search or following signals from other cell types, employ efficient search strategies, follow chemokine gradients during priming in lymph nodes, and that NK cells can recruit CTLs indirectly via dendritic cells. Intravital microscopy is typically restricted to short imaging periods and sub-millimeter fields of view.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These provide important context for the novelty of the current findings but are not results of this study.

results.result: The findings are contextualized within prior literature on chemotaxis, desensitization, GPCR signaling, neutrophil swarming, T cell priming in lymph nodes, quorum sensing, bystander recruitment, hot vs. cold tumours, and alternative chemokine signaling circuits (CXCR3, BLT1). CCR5-expressing CTLs have been associated with autoimmune diseases and viral hyperinflammation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C39-C40, C79, C83-C84, C87, C94, C96-C97, C100-C104 accurately cite and contextualize prior work. These are appropriately used to frame the current findings and discuss implications, but are not novel results of this study.

results.result: The authors discuss implications and limitations: CCR5-mediated recruitment is likely not the only signaling circuit for tumour infiltration; CTLs can independently induce mass recruitment; lymphocytes can recruit distant lymphocytes directly; CTLs engaging non-cognate targets induce chemokinesis; the recruitment signal is generic despite antigen-specific production; and the mechanism could be exploited therapeutically.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C85-C86, C88, C95, C98-C99, C105 represent appropriate discussion of implications, limitations, and future directions. These are well-grounded in the data but include speculative elements (C70, C88, C105) that are appropriately qualified. C98-C99 summarize in vivo findings.
